title: Make HIPAA Compliant: 7 Steps to Follow (2026 Guide)
summary: To make HIPAA compliant, businesses need technical safeguards and policies—not certificates. You'll know the seven required steps for your organization.
body_markdown:
## Seven Steps to Make a Business HIPAA Compliant


**Seven steps, taken in order, make a business HIPAA compliant, and the second one, the written risk analysis, is the step that matters most because every later decision depends on it.**


The sequence below shows what each step produces, so that at the end you hold seven documents an auditor can ask for and you can hand over.


HHS builds its Security Rule guidance around the same logic: know what you hold, assess the risk, then act on what you found.


Each step below names the artifact it should leave behind.


Artifact: a PHI inventory. List every system, device, vendor and automation that creates, stores or transmits protected health information. Include the unglamorous places, such as shared inboxes, spreadsheets and scanned forms.


Anything missing here is invisible to every later step, so it becomes an unassessed risk. Small practices can finish this quickly; larger ones need interviews with each department.


### Step 2: Complete a written risk analysis


Artifact: a dated risk analysis document. For each item in the inventory, record the threat, how likely it is, the impact, and the safeguard in place. Name the person who signed it.


Most penalties trace back to this step: an organization with good tools but no documented analysis can't show it knew what it was protecting. Budget the most time here, and expect it to be the longest stage.


### Step 3: Apply administrative, physical and technical safeguards


Artifact: a remediation record tied to the risk analysis. Access controls, encryption, audit logging, locked equipment and workforce sanctions all belong here, but only as responses to risks you identified.


Every control should point back to a line in the analysis. Spending on a control with no matching risk has no evidence behind it.


### Step 4: Sign business associate agreements


Artifact: a signed agreement for every vendor that touches PHI. This covers cloud hosts, billing services and any automation platform that moves patient data.


Where a vendor won't sign, the data shouldn't go to that vendor. Treat each new connection as a liability until the agreement is on file.


### Step 5: Write policies and train staff


Artifact: written policies and a training log. Policies state who may see what and what happens when rules are broken.


The log records who was trained, on what, and when. Training without a record can't be shown to anyone, so for audit purposes it didn't happen.


### Step 6: Prepare a breach response plan


Artifact: a breach response plan. Define who decides whether an incident is a reportable breach, who notifies patients and regulators, and how evidence is kept. Test it once with a realistic scenario, because a plan first read during an incident is a draft.


### Step 7: Document everything and review annually


Artifact: a review file. Revisit the inventory and risk analysis at least yearly and whenever you add a system, vendor or workflow. Keep the previous versions, since the history of your decisions is the evidence of compliance.
